title: U.S. Naval Academy Program Conducts Operations with Hurricane Hunters
description: ANNAPOLIS, Md. (Oct. 19, 2022) Capt. Beth Sanabia, a professor at the U.S. Naval Academy, and midshipmen participating in her Training and Research in Oceanic and Atmospheric Processes in Tropical Cyclones (TROPIC) program fly into Hurricane Ian to collect data under the ocean for use in the predictions of future storms, Sept. 28. (U.S. Navy video by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Jordyn Diomede)
keywords: USNA, Oceanography, Tropic, Hurricane Ian, Hurricane Hunters, research

transcript.text: My name is Captain Beth Stenabia. I'm a permanent military professor here in the Oceanography Department at the Naval Academy.
Tropic is a program here at the Naval Academy and it stands for training and research in oceanographic and
atmospheric processes in tropical cyclones.
In the Naval Academy portion of it, we take Mitch Whitman down to fly with the hurricane hunters.
And so the Air Force Hurricane Hunters in their program, they deploy
atmospheric sensors to measure the atmosphere in hurricanes and around the immediate hurricane environment.
And our role in that program is to measure the ocean underneath the storm.
So after the brief, we would go out onto the aircraft and we'd set up and the Mitch will run the equipment.
We will deploy ocean sensors and so that they're called AXP keys for airborne expendable bath
of thermographs and the Navy has used them for decades to measure the temperature of the ocean under the storm.
So they are used to help the initial conditions for the models so that when the forecasts are run,
they have better conditions to work with and so hopefully that will
positively impact the forecasts that the models give to the hurricane center so the
forecasters at the hurricane center can make better decisions.
The science mission is what we accomplished while we're there.
So we did that by deploying sensors, processing the data and sending that data off for
assimilation into the numerical models.
After that, we will then do research on the data that we collected.
We are incredibly grateful to
the faculty, staff, and others here at the Academy who support this program.
I'm incredibly grateful to them as well as the Department for supporting this a number of years over.

Not just for the development of Mitch and then
although clearly that's one of our priorities but to address scientific problems which are relevant to the Navy.
If you step back like the biggest
thing here and the most important thing is that we keep our ships at sea safe and we keep our folks ashore safe and
not just in the military but in
anywhere along the coast because the storms are significant, they're devastating and
the better we can make those forecasts, the better we can make the models that make the forecast.
Hopefully we can
improve them to the point where people
really know early on when they're in danger and can take actions like effective actions to prepare and to
leave if they need to and follow the direction of the emergency personnel.
But we can just help the forecasters who are doing a great job down the Earth and Sun.
